 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. INDIANAPOLIS – As widely-panned as his unflinching decision may be, Colts head coach Shane Steichen 's choice to back Daniel Jones as his starting quarterback is of his own accord.
 Unlike her father, the late longtime Colts team owner Jim Irsay , chose to influence the team's direction at quarterback – moving on from Peyton Manning to Andrew Luck , benching Matt Ryan for Sam Ehlinger and demanding the team draft a quarterback in 2023 among them – Indianapolis principal team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon has not put her finger on the scale, despite Jones' abysmal play for a 3-7 team.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I've had those conversations with her, but she lets me go," Steichen said Monday, in reference to his weekly meetings with his boss and the team's quarterback conundrum.

(Grace Hollars/IndyStar) Steichen offered no new reasoning Monday when peppered by reporters to defend about his backing of Jones, who threw two more interceptions Sunday in the Colts' 24-22 win. Jones' completions (11), completion percentage (.500), interceptions and interception percentage (.091) from Sunday all were season worsts, and the totality of his performance – perhaps best measured by passer rating – graded as the third-worst game of the 2019 No. 6 pick's eight-year career.
 According to ESPN, Jones' 1.7 QBR mark from Sunday against the 1-8 Dolphins was the worst of any starting quarterback this season. In his first career start (or NFL regular-season appearance of any kind), Miami quarterback Kyle McCord finished 17-for-32 for 209 yards and no turnovers. His passer rating (73.6) was close to double that of Jones (41.5).
 And yet, just about any time he's asked about Jones' inefficiencies, Steichen chooses to emphasize that issues and mistakes spread well beyond Jones.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "There's a lot of things that play into it. Obviously, (Jones) knows he needs to take care of the ball better, first and foremost," Steichen said. "I think it's not all about one guy. It takes all 11 to do the job at a high level, and that starts with me as a playcaller calling better plays and making sure guys are getting open and separating.
 "He does lead our team each and every week to get ready for games on Sunday."
 The questions about Jones began after a worrisome Week 4 performance in London, where he had two early turnovers and finished with a completion percentage below 60% and fewer than 150 yards for the first time this season. Since then, Jones has completed at least 60% of his throws once. The league average is 63.9%. Only twice since Week 4 has Jones had games with more than 180 yards passing. Among 30 players who've made at least five starts this season, the 15th-best season average is 235.3 passing yards per game. And Jones has these shortcomings while operating alongside the NFL's 10th-best rushing attack.
 As woeful as the season-long stats are – Jones ranks 28th in completion percentage, interception percentage, QBR, yards per completion and yards per game; 30th in yards per attempt and touchdown percentage; and dead last (31st) in passer rating – Jones' decision-making may be his most detrimental stat of all. The Colts starter leads the league in interceptions (12) and total turnovers (15). 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Steichen has maintained that Jones gives the Colts the best chance to win, and he has constantly praised Jones' preparation even though it has not led to an uptick in performance.
 Steichen maintains he holds his starting quarterback accountable and staunchly denies that Jones is treated differently than his teammates.
 "I have those conversations with him. I have game reviews on Mondays and show the clips where we've all got to be better, and that's not just him; that's everybody involved that has a part in it," Steichen said. "I treat all my players the same. Obviously, quarterback is different no matter who the starting quarterback is. Obviously, it's a different position and a unique position, more than any other position.
 "But I do treat all the players the same."
